craft_claim: A voice that addresses the self from outside — third person, second person, or an observer stance — turns raw feeling into generalisable reflection without tipping into rumination.

supporting_evidence.location: Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 55, pp. 81-136
supporting_evidence.note: The review distinguishes self-immersed rumination from self-distanced reflection and reports that adopting an observer stance produces more adaptive, less reactive analysis of negative experience.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 106(2), pp. 304-324
supporting_evidence.note: Shifting self-talk away from first person acts as a regulatory mechanism, supporting the linguistic route by which an observer stance is enacted on the page.

supporting_evidence.location: Passim, e.g. the self-addressed entries of Books 2-4
supporting_evidence.note: The Meditations are written as second-person or impersonal self-address that converts a daily irritation into a principle about conduct and mortality.

scope: First-person reflective and academic prose, and philosophical fiction that needs to hold feeling at reflective distance.
exceptions: Self-distancing can become evasion or emotional flatness when used to avoid a stake that the reader has already been promised (compare tone-detached).
